summary: Proposal from the IETF Point-to-Point Protocol Working Group for multi-protocol transmission of datagrams over point-to-point links, aimed at advancing PPP toward draft standard. It was replaced by RFC 1171.

eli5.summary: If two computers share one wire, they need rules for taking turns and packing messages. This is a first proposal for those rules.

subtitle: A protocol framework for transmitting multiple network protocols over serial point-to-point links.

tldr.problem: While most networked hosts connect via LANs or WANs, point-to-point links like dial-ups lack a standard protocol for reliably encapsulating and managing multiple network protocols.
tldr.mechanism: PPP provides three components: an HDLC-based encapsulation scheme for framing data, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) to establish and configure the connection, and Network Control Protocols (NCPs) to configure individual network-layer protocols like IP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1134 proposed the initial PPP design, which was later refined and superseded by RFC 1171.

today: RFC 1171 superseded this proposal with refinements to the PPP design.

sections.title: The Problem with Point-to-Point Links
sections.content:
Most TCP/IP hosts connect via Local Area Networks (LANs) like Ethernet or Wide Area Networks (WANs) like X.25, which have standard protocols. However, point-to-point connections—simple serial links between two machines, such as RS-232-C asynchronous interfaces—are ubiquitous yet lack an agreed-upon encapsulation standard. The Internet has various non-standard implementations but no Internet Standard for these links.

Beyond encapsulation, point-to-point links create special challenges. IP address assignment is difficult on switched circuits like dial-ups. The protocol must handle asynchronous (start-stop) and synchronous transmission, multiplex different network protocols, negotiate optional features like data compression, and test link quality.
sections.eli5: Almost every computer can connect through a single serial cable, but there's no official rulebook. This document proposes one, including how to handle special cases like slow connections or compression.

sections.title: Three-Layer Design
sections.content:
PPP organizes the protocol into three parts working together. The Physical Layer accepts any duplex serial circuit (dedicated or switched), supporting both asynchronous and synchronous modes. No special modem control signals are required, though they may improve performance.

The Data Link Layer uses HDLC principles to frame datagrams. Each frame begins and ends with a Flag byte (0x7e), contains an Address byte (always 0xff, the all-stations address), a Control byte (always 0x03 for unnumbered information), a two-byte Protocol field identifying the packet type (ranging from 0x0021 for IP to 0xc021 for the Link Control Protocol itself), the data payload, and a 16-bit Frame Check Sequence for error detection.

The Control Layers consist of the Link Control Protocol (LCP) to establish and manage the link itself, and Network Control Protocols (NCPs) such as IPCP to negotiate per-protocol settings. Once the physical link is up, LCP packets configure the connection, then NCPs configure individual network protocols.
sections.eli5: Think of three nested envelopes: the outermost handles the physical connection, the middle one wraps each message with markers so the receiver knows where it starts and stops, and the innermost negotiates what kind of data can be sent.

sections.title: Link Control Protocol Negotiation
sections.content:
The Link Control Protocol operates as a finite-state machine moving through seven states. The connection begins Closed. Upon an Active-Open command, the originator sends a Configure-Request packet and enters the Request-Sent state, waiting for a response. The responder in the Listen state sends its own Configure-Request.

Once both sides have sent and received Configure-Ack packets (positive responses), the link enters the Open state and data may flow. The state machine differentiates between acceptable and unacceptable configuration options: a Configure-Nak suggests alternative values, while a Configure-Reject refuses certain options. Restart timers prevent livelocks from missed packets; implementations default to 3-second timeouts and should retry up to 10 times before declaring the link dead.

LCP packets include Code, Identifier, and Length fields, plus option data. Codes 1-4 handle configuration negotiation (Request, Ack, Nak, Reject), codes 5-6 terminate the link, and codes 7-11 manage errors and testing (Code-Reject, Protocol-Reject, Echo-Request, Echo-Reply, Discard-Request). Configuration Options modify default behavior (such as maximum receive unit or authentication method) and are described in separate documents.
sections.eli5: Before data flows, both computers exchange messages: 'Here's what I can do' and 'Okay, I agree' or 'Can you change that setting?' They keep trying until they agree, then the connection opens.

sections.title: Configuring Network Protocols
sections.content:
Once the Link Control Protocol opens the connection, Network Control Protocols (NCPs) configure individual network-layer protocols. The IP Control Protocol (IPCP) handles Internet Protocol. It is identical to LCP except that it uses Protocol field value 0x8021, restricts itself to codes 1-7 (configuration and termination only, no echo or discard), and waits for the optional Link Quality Determination phase of LCP to complete.

IPCP negotiates configuration options specific to IP, such as IP address assignment. The RFC reserves option definitions for separate documents. Once IPCP reaches the Open state, IP datagrams flow using Protocol field value 0x0021. The maximum IP packet size is the same as the PPP Information field size; larger datagrams must be fragmented.
sections.eli5: After the basic connection is open, each type of data (like Internet packets) gets its own setup conversation. For Internet, both computers say what IP addresses they'll use, then start sending packets.

sections.title: Supporting Asynchronous Links
sections.content:
ISO 3309-1979 defines HDLC for synchronous links. For asynchronous links (where bits are framed with start and stop bits), PPP uses modifications from ISO 3309:1984/PDAD1, a Proposed Draft International Standard. The key challenge is transparency: certain byte values conflict with the HDLC protocol (like the 0x7e Flag and the 0x7d Control Escape). To transmit these safely, the sender replaces the Flag, Control Escape, and any byte below 0x20 (ASCII control characters) with a two-byte sequence: the Control Escape (0x7d) followed by the original byte XORed with 0x20. The receiver reverses this after receiving.

For example, a Flag byte 0x7e is transmitted as 0x7d 0x5e, and a Control Escape is transmitted as 0x7d 0x5d. This ensures that terminal equipment and data network modems, many of which filter control characters, cannot corrupt PPP frames. On asynchronous links, frames may be aborted by framing errors (a stop bit where a 1-bit is expected) or by a Control Escape immediately followed by a closing Flag. Inter-frame time fill uses continuous 1-bits (mark-hold).
sections.eli5: Asynchronous serial links use special characters to mark control signals, which would break the protocol if they appear in the data. To fix this, certain bytes get wrapped in a special 'escape' sequence so the receiver knows they're data, not control signals.
